subject: Accounting
title: Free Cash Flow
description: A quick, practical guide to Free Cash Flow.

hook.text: After paying for operations and maintaining assets, how much cash is truly left over?

buildup.text: Free cash flow subtracts capital expenditures from operating cash flow.

discovery.text: It's the cash available for dividends, buybacks, debt payoff, or new investments.

twist.text: Buffett loves free cash flow. He says it reveals what owners can actually take home.

climax.text: Companies with strong free cash flow have choices. Those without are trapped.

punchline.text: Free cash flow is the real measure of financial freedom.

quiz.question: How is free cash flow calculated?
options: Operating cash flow minus capital expenditures

details.summary: Free cash flow measures the cash a company generates after accounting for capital expenditures needed to maintain and grow its asset base. This topic explains why FCF is often considered more reliable than net income for evaluating a company's financial health.
details.whyItMatters: Net income can be manipulated through accounting choices. Free cash flow is harder to fake because it measures actual cash generated—the real economic output of a business.
takeaways: Free cash flow equals operating cash flow minus capital expenditures
Consistently positive FCF means the company generates more cash than it needs to maintain operations
Companies with strong FCF can pay dividends, buy back shares, reduce debt, or fund acquisitions without borrowing

faq.question: How is free cash flow calculated?
faq.answer: Free cash flow equals cash flow from operations minus capital expenditures. Some analysts also subtract mandatory debt payments. It represents the cash available after the business has invested what's needed to maintain and grow its productive capacity.

faq.question: Why do analysts prefer free cash flow over net income?
faq.answer: Net income includes non-cash items like depreciation and can be affected by accounting policy choices. Free cash flow measures actual cash generated, which is harder to manipulate. A company with growing net income but declining FCF is a warning sign.
